questions.text: Suppose n and p are unsigned int variables in a C program. We wish to set p to [latex]^nC_3[/latex]. If n is large, which one of the following statements is most likely to set p correctly?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- Option 1: n(n[latex]-[/latex]1)(n[latex]-[/latex]2) is computed first, which overflows for large n.
- Option 2: n(n[latex]-[/latex]1)/2 is always an exact integer; multiplying by (n[latex]-[/latex]2) gives a multiple of 3, so /3 is also exact. Intermediate values stay small.
- Option 3: n(n[latex]-[/latex]1)/3 need not be exact (e.g. n = 5: 20/3), so truncation gives wrong result.
- Option 4: divides by 2 and then by 6, i.e. by 12 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] wrong.

Answer: p = n * (n - 1) / 2 * (n-2) / 3;

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.text:
Consider the following pseudo code. What is the total number of multiplications to be performed? 
 D= 2
for i = 1 to n do
   for j = i to n do
      for k = j + 1 to n do
           D = D * 3
questions.solution:
For fixed i and j the innermost loop runs n [latex]-[/latex] j times. Summing over [latex]1\le i\le j\le n[/latex] gives [latex]\binom{n+1}{3}=\frac{(n-1)n(n+1)}{6}[/latex].

That is one-sixth of the product of 3 consecutive integers.

Answer: One-sixth of the product of the 3 consecutive integers

Y starts as the sum of the whole array (which is itself a sub-array). The loops compute the sum Z of every sub-array E[i..j] and keep the largest. So the result is the maximum sub-array sum.

Answer: maximum possible sum of elements in any sub-array of array E
